name: Failed Project Analysis
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Three Autopsies: TradeLens, the ASX CHESS Replacement, and Diem
lesson.summary: Looking closely at how three well-funded, well-publicized blockchain projects actually died shows that the causes were rarely cryptographic or technical, they were consortium governance, project execution, and regulatory collision, exactly the kinds of limitations the earlier chapters identified.
lesson.body:
Failures are systematically underreported compared to launch announcements, which is exactly why the case-study-analysis checklist insists on checking whether a project is still running years later. This chapter applies that checklist in reverse, looking closely at three prominent blockchain projects that did not survive, to identify which structural limitation from the previous chapter each one actually traces back to.

The first is TradeLens, introduced in the supply chain chapter. Maersk and IBM shut the platform down in 2022, stating publicly that it had not achieved the level of industry-wide collaboration needed to be commercially viable, even though the underlying technology functioned as designed. The root cause was governance, not cryptography: competing shipping lines did not want to run critical parts of their own operations on infrastructure that looked, structurally, like it was owned and controlled by their largest competitor. No amount of better engineering could have fixed a problem that was fundamentally about who gets to be seen as neutral.

The second is the Australian Securities Exchange's long attempt to replace its aging CHESS clearing and settlement system with a distributed ledger platform, built together with Digital Asset using its DAML smart contract language, an effort that ran for roughly seven years starting in the mid-2010s. The project suffered repeated delays and was ultimately scrapped in November 2022, after an independent review found the replacement system was not fit for purpose; public reporting at the time described a financial write-down in the hundreds of millions of Australian dollars, though readers should treat the precise figure as something to verify rather than take as exact. The root cause here looks different from TradeLens: by most public accounts, it was a mix of underestimated engineering complexity for a system that sits at the core of a national financial market, and unclear or shifting requirements and governance within the project itself, rather than a fundamental flaw in distributed ledger technology as such. It is worth noting that Digital Asset's underlying technology continued to be used in other financial infrastructure projects elsewhere, which supports treating this as a project-specific execution failure rather than proof that the technology cannot ever work for market infrastructure.

The third is Diem, covered in the financial services chapter, and it is the cleanest example of all three of a failure with essentially nothing to do with engineering. Diem's core technical work was largely complete. What ended the project was that regulators and legislators around the world were unwilling to let a private consortium led by Facebook issue an instrument that functioned like a global currency, seeing it as a direct challenge to monetary sovereignty. No case-study checklist focused on technology readiness would have flagged this risk, because it was never a technology problem; it was a collision between corporate ambition and the authority of national governments over their own money.

Three different projects, three different root causes, consortium governance, project execution and requirements, and regulatory collision, and none of them a cryptographic failure. That reinforces the lesson from the previous chapter on successful adoption factors from the opposite direction: across well-funded projects with serious corporate backing, technology readiness was rarely the limiting factor. Organizational readiness, competitive dynamics, and legal and political readiness were.
